did_you_know.text: The name "Tent of Meeting" literally describes a tent for a special encounter. It refers to the designated place where God speaks with Moses.
The Hebrew word korban is related to the root meaning "to draw near." An offering is therefore presented not only as a gift, but also as a way of drawing closer to God.
Here, the word tamim does not mean morally perfect; it describes an animal that is whole and free of physical defects. In this chapter, it refers mainly to the animal’s physical condition.
The name olah is related to the Hebrew root meaning "to rise." It likely refers to the smoke rising from the altar, and in this offering the entire animal was burned.

Turtledoves and young pigeons provided an offering option for people who did not bring cattle or sheep. In chapter 5, the Torah explicitly connects birds with people who could not afford a larger animal.
Near the altar there was a designated place called "the ash heap," where waste and ashes were removed. The altar service therefore included organization and cleaning, not only burning the offering.
